summary.text: Hiring a Tyrrhenian ship to cross from Icaria to Naxos, Dionysus was carried past the island toward a slaver's market — until he turned the mast to snakes, the sails to vine-leaves, and the crew to dolphins leaping in the sea.

chapters.title: The hired ship
chapters.text: Wishing to be ferried across from Icaria to Naxos, Dionysus hired a pirate ship of Tyrrhenians. They took him aboard, but instead of making for the island they sailed past Naxos and steered for Asia, intending to sell the beautiful youth as a slave.

chapters.title: Acoetes' warning
chapters.text: Acoetes the pilot alone saw the truth. In Ovid he is a Maeonian fisherman who tells the crew the prisoner is no mortal boy: vines had twined the mast, ivy bound the oars, and panthers lurked in the hold. Hyginus says when the Tyrrhenians wished to debauch Liber because of his beauty, Acoetes restrained them and suffered at their hands — the only sailor Liber would spare.

chapters.title: Vines, flutes, and dolphins
chapters.text: The god revealed himself. Apollodorus says he turned the mast and oars into snakes and filled the vessel with ivy and the sound of flutes; the pirates went mad, leaped into the sea, and were changed into dolphins. Ovid has lions and panthers burst from the deck while the sailors' limbs grow finny scales; Hyginus changes oars to thyrsi and sails to vine-leaves, and from that day dolphins were called Tyrrhenians.

chapters.title: Thyone and heaven
chapters.text: Thus men perceived that Dionysus was a god and honored him. Apollodorus closes the wandering with the god's apotheosis of his mother: having brought Semele up from Hades and named her Thyone, he ascended with her to heaven — the twice-born completing the circuit from pirate sea to Olympian triumph.
